bib.title: Language Models of Code are Few-Shot Commonsense Learners
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 2022 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), pages 1384-1403

question: Do large language models of code, prompted with the output graph rewritten as Python, generate structured commonsense graphs better than natural-language LLMs prompted with serialized text graphs?
hypothesis: Code-LLMs can be repurposed to generate structured output better than NL-LLMs, because code-formatted graphs resemble their pre-training data.
contributions: Insight that Code-LLMs are better structured commonsense reasoners than NL-LLMs when the desired graph is represented as code.
CoCoGen: a method for using Code-LLMs for structured commonsense generation.
Evaluation on three structured commonsense generation tasks showing CoCoGen outperforms fine-tuned and few-shot NL-LLMs while controlling for number of task examples.
Ablations on data formatting, model size and number of few-shot examples.

method.summary: Each (text input T, graph G) pair is rewritten as a Python class or function (nodes as objects, edges as attributes or add_edge calls). A few such classes form a few-shot prompt for Codex (code-davinci-002); the test input is a partial class that the model completes, and the code is parsed back into a graph. Baselines are text-davinci-002 and text-curie-001 given the same examples as flattened text, and fine-tuned T5.
method.task: structured commonsense generation (script generation, edge prediction, entity state tracking, explanation graph generation)

datasets.name: ProScript
datasets.split: test split obtained from the authors of ProScript
datasets.source: Sakaguchi et al. 2021; DAGs from ROCStories, Descript, VirtualHome
datasets.preprocessing: each node becomes a Node() instance, edges as children attribute; for edge prediction nodes are listed in random order

datasets.name: ProPara
datasets.preprocessing: main function with actions as comments, state_k variables per entity, one function per action plus init; UNK for unknown location, None for non-existence

datasets.name: ExplaGraphs
datasets.preprocessing: belief, argument, stance as strings; edges as add_edge(source, edge_type, destination); begin list of start nodes; stance taken from the stance predictor released by Saha et al.

other.note: Appendix A estimates capacity only via loss per token: Codex 0.46 code / 2.71 text

models.name: text-curie-001 (CURIE)
models.architecture: GPT-3 based NL model, smaller than DAVINCI

models.name: T5-large (ExplaGraphs) / T5-xxl (ProScript, results from Sakaguchi et al. 2021)

other.note: fine-tuned on the task data; T5 sizes as named, parameter counts not printed

inference.samples: ProScript and ExplaGraphs: at least 3 different prompts, averaged; Appendix I: 3 random seeds that set example order; ProPara: 5 runs with different randomly sampled prompts
inference.prompting: few-shot: prompt p is k Python classes (T, Gc) concatenated; test input appended as partial class; k randomly sampled from training set, k between 5 and 30 depending on task (15 ProScript, 3 ProPara, 30 ExplaGraphs); GPT-3 baselines get the same examples as flattened text
inference.retrieval: optional dynamic prompt: KST retriever (mpnet-base) fetches k nearest training examples; trained with L = (cos(f(Ti), f(Tj)) - sim(Gi, Gj))^2

other.decoding_settings: temperature, top_p, max output tokens and decoding strategy not stated in the paper

metrics.name: BLEU / ROUGE-L / BLEURT
metrics.definition: content overlap of generated vs reference script

metrics.name: GED
metrics.definition: number of node/edge edits to transform generated graph into reference

metrics.name: ISO
metrics.definition: fraction of generated graphs isomorphic to the reference, ignoring node text

metrics.name: Edge prediction P/R/F1
metrics.definition: precision, recall, F1 of predicted edge set vs true (paper prints r = |E union E^|/|E|, which looks like a typo)

metrics.name: ProPara entity-state P/R/F1
metrics.definition: precision/recall/F1 of predicted entity states (Dalvi et al. 2018)

metrics.name: StCA, SeCA, G-BS, GED, EA
metrics.definition: Saha et al. 2021 metrics: structural accuracy (connected DAGs with two concepts from belief and argument), learned semantic correctness, G-BERTScore, graph edit distance, edge importance accuracy

baselines: T5 fine-tuned (100, 1k, 4k examples on edge prediction; 150, 1500, 2500 on ExplaGraphs)
eval.protocol: At least 3 prompts averaged; std in Appendix I; improvements over DAVINCI reported significant at p < 0.001 (test not named). Human eval: 20 samples, three of the authors, pairwise blind choice on relevance and correctness.

availability.data: prompts and model outputs in the same repository

prompts.purpose: ProScript script generation, partial class given at test time
ExplaGraphs prompt format (Literal example, completion starts after '# Edges')
prompts.text:
class ExplanationDAG:
    def __init__(self):
        belief = "factory farming should not be banned."
        argument = "Factory farming feeds millions."
        stance = "support"
        # Edges
        begin = ["factory farming", "millions"]
        add_edge("factory farming", "causes", "food")

evidence.quote: In our experiments, k varies between 5 and 30

results.claim: On ProScript script generation, CoCoGen with 15 prompt examples beats T5 fine-tuned on all 3500 samples on BLEU.
results.setup: ProScript test, Codex code-davinci-002, 15-shot random prompts, Python Tree class; T5 fine-tuned on full training data
results.quote: outperforms the fine-tuned model T5 which has been fine-tuned on all 3500 samples
results.table: Table 1, row COCOGEN (15), column BLEU (25.24); row T5 (fine-tuned) 23.80
results.note: Text says 3500 samples; Table 12 lists 3252 train

results.claim: On ProScript edge prediction, CoCoGen (15 examples) reaches F1 56.24, above DAVINCI (48.92) and T5 fine-tuned on 1k (60.15 is higher; CoCoGen is above T5 on 100 at 51.89).
results.setup: ProScript edge prediction, 15-shot, Codex code-davinci-002, Python Tree prompt
results.quote: COCOGEN with only 15 examples outperforms the fine-tuned T5 which was fine-tuned on 100 examples
results.table: Table 2, row COCOGEN (15), column F1 (56.24); row DAVINCI (15) 48.92; row T5 (100) 51.89
results.note: Table 2 caption claims outperforming T5 on 1k samples, but T5 (1k) F1 is 60.15 > 56.24; the body text claims only T5 (100). Table 5 and Table 6 print the same CoCoGen F1 as 56.52, Table 19 as 56.2.

results.claim: On ProPara with 3 shots, CoCoGen gets F1 63.0, 5.0 higher than DAVINCI and 74% higher than CURIE.
results.setup: ProPara, 3 random training examples in prompt, Codex code-davinci-002 vs text-davinci-002 and text-curie-001
results.quote: COCOGEN achieves a significantly better F1 score than DAVINCI. Across the five prompts, COCOGEN achieves 5.0 higher F1 than DAVINCI on average.
results.table: Table 3, row COCOGEN, column F1 (63.0); row DAVINCI 58.0; row CURIE 36.1
results.note: Appendix Table 21 prints CoCoGen 62.8 +/- 2.4 and DAVINCI 56.9 +/- 2.4 across three seeds.

results.claim: CoCoGen is state-of-the-art in the few-shot setting on ProPara and under 10 F1 below the overall SOTA, which fine-tunes on the full training set.
results.setup: ProPara leaderboard as of 10/11/2022; CoCoGen would rank 6th
results.quote: In the few-shot settings, COCOGEN is state-of-the-art in PROPARA.

results.claim: On ExplaGraphs, CoCoGen with 30 examples beats T5 fine-tuned on 1500 examples on all metrics; structural accuracy 45.20 vs 38.19.
results.setup: ExplaGraphs eval split, Codex code-davinci-002, 30-shot random prompts, Python ExplanationDAG class
results.quote: COCOGEN with only 30 examples outperforms the T5 model that was fine-tuned using 1500 examples, across all metrics.
results.table: Table 4, row COCOGEN (30), column StCA (45.20); row T5 (1500) 38.19
results.note: Table 4 shows DAVINCI (30) StCA 23.62 and T5 (2500) 43.22.

results.claim: Both the code model and the code prompt matter, and together they help more than the sum of each alone: on ExplaGraphs StCA, DAVINCI+text 33.16, DAVINCI+code 33.00, Codex+text 38.02, CoCoGen 45.20.
results.setup: ExplaGraphs and ProScript edge prediction, 2x2 of model (DAVINCI vs Codex) and prompt (text vs code)
results.quote: However when using both a Code-LLM and a code prompt – the improvement is greater than the sum
results.table: Table 5, row CODEX + text, column StCA (38.02); row DAVINCI + text 33.16
results.note: Table 5 gives DAVINCI+code SeCA 15.37 vs text 7.14; edge-prediction F1 43.06 / 49.3 / 44.47 / 56.52.

results.claim: Dynamic prompt retrieval (KST) raises ProScript edge-prediction F1 from 56.52 to 65.71.
results.setup: ProScript edge prediction, 15-shot, mpnet-base retriever fine-tuned with KST loss vs random prompt
results.quote: Our retrieval mechanism is highly effective for
results.table: Table 6, row COCOGEN + KST, column F1 (65.71); row COCOGEN 56.52

results.claim: KST retrieval hurts ExplaGraphs: StCA falls from 45.2 to 37.47, because nearest neighbours in the training set are near-duplicates and cut prompt diversity.
results.setup: ExplaGraphs eval, CoCoGen + code-davinci-002 with KST-retrieved prompts vs random
results.table: Table 9, row COCOGEN + 002 + KST, column StCA (37.47); row COCOGEN + 002 45.2

results.claim: KST gives only marginal gains on ProScript script generation (BLEU 25.24 to 25.4).
results.setup: ProScript script generation, 15-shot, Codex-002 with KST
results.quote: Dynamically creating a prompt leads to marginal improvements.
results.table: Table 8, row COCOGEN + 002 (15) + KST, column BLEU (25.4)

results.claim: The Python class format matters, and the best format depends on the task: on ExplaGraphs the Literal format (StCA 45.2) beats Tree (39.24) and Relation (42.82).
results.setup: ExplaGraphs, Codex-002, three Python formats from Figure 7
results.quote: there are no clear task-agnostic Python class designs that work uniformly well
results.table: Table 13, row CODEX-002 Tree, column StCA (39.24)
results.note: On ProScript edge prediction (Table 14) CODEX-002 Tree F1 56.5 vs Literal 52.0, though the caption says literal performs best; on script generation (Table 15) Literal BLEU 25.24 beats Tree 18.96.

results.claim: Larger Codex is less sensitive to prompt format: Codex-001 swings from F1 15.9 (Literal) to 29.7 (Tree) on edge prediction, while Codex-002 swings from 52.0 to 56.5.
results.setup: ProScript edge prediction, identical prompts, code-davinci-001 vs 002
results.quote: as model size increases, the sensitivity of the model on the prompt reduces
results.table: Table 14, row CODEX-001 Literal, column F1 (15.9)
results.note: Model size is inferred from the API's description of 002 as most capable, not stated numerically.

results.claim: Code-davinci-002 beats code-davinci-001 on ProScript script generation with identical prompts (BLEU 25.24 vs 22.9).
In a blind pairwise human evaluation on 20 ExplaGraphs samples, CoCoGen graphs were preferred for correctness 38.3% vs 18.3% for DAVINCI.
results.setup: ExplaGraphs and ProScript script generation, CoCoGen vs DAVINCI, annotators could pick no preference (31.7% for ExplaGraphs correctness)
results.table: Table 11, row EXPLAGRAPHS under Correctness, column COCOGEN (38.3%)
results.note: For ProScript the preferences are close (26.7% vs 23.3% on correctness), with 50% no preference.

results.claim: Across three seeds, CoCoGen's improvements over DAVINCI are reported significant (p < 0.001); ProScript script-generation BLEU 25.3 +/- 0.1 vs 23.1 +/- 2.7.
results.setup: ProScript script generation, seeds set the order of examples in the prompt
results.quote: all improvements of COCOGEN over DAVINCI are statistically significant (p-value < 0.001)
results.note: Seeds vary example order; Section 3.1 says prompts are resampled (at least 3 different prompts). Significance test not named.

results.claim: Codex nearly always generates syntactically valid Python that converts back into a graph.
results.setup: CoCoGen on all three tasks with code-davinci-002
results.quote: we used CODEX (Chen et al., 2021a) and found that it nearly always generates syntactically valid Python.
results.note: Appendix E: nearly 100% of cases, no exact rate given

results.claim: Codex has lower code loss per token than DAVINCI (0.46 vs 0.63) but higher text loss (2.71 vs 2.25), used to argue the two are comparable in capacity.
results.unit: nats per token (inferred, unit not printed)
results.n: 30 random Wikiplots pages for text; Polycoder eval split Python for code
results.setup: Appendix A size estimate for Codex, DAVINCI, CURIE
results.quote: CODEX and DAVINCI are of comparable capacities

limits: Models (Codex, DAVINCI, CURIE) are closed; pretraining corpus, size and biases are undocumented, so size comparisons are educated guesses (Appendix A).
Authors are unsure Codex will remain free for research; Codex has since been deprecated by OpenAI (not stated in the paper).
The ExplaGraphs test split was unavailable, so results are on the validation split.
Python format must be designed per task; no format works uniformly.
Dynamic prompt retrieval helps edge prediction but hurts ExplaGraphs because of near-duplicate training examples.
Human evaluation is 20 examples judged by three of the authors.
Decoding settings (temperature, max tokens) are not reported, and the CURIE ProPara result suffers from output-format failures (high precision, low recall).
Internal inconsistencies: edge-prediction caption claims a win over T5 (1k) that Table 2 does not show; the Table 14 caption disagrees with its numbers.

terms.definition: models of Code for Commonsense Generation: frame the output structure as Python code and prompt a Code-LLM few-shot
structure converted into text, such as a flat list of node pairs or a DOT string
a retriever fine-tuned so that embedding similarity of inputs matches similarity of their output graphs, used to pick prompt examples
